title: Calgary's ageing sewers, and how long sewer pipes last around the world
subtitle: The age and material of every public sanitary service connection, compared with expected service lives from Canada, Australia, the UK and Germany
question: Give me a comprehensive report on the ageing sewerage system of Calgary and compare it with the usual life of sewer pipes worldwide. Include a map of Calgary communities shaded by the main measure.
summary: The typical public sewer connection in Calgary is **31 years** old (half were laid before 1995); **24.8%** (91,258) are more than 50 years old.
Measured against typical service lives used by utilities, **32,720** connections (8.9%) are already past theirs; on cautious lives it is **94,697** (25.8%).
Clay tile is the swing factor: **74,089** connections, mostly from the 1960s and 1970s; three in four are past a 50-year life but almost none past 100 years.
Communities with sewers 60 years or older report **48.02** sewage back-ups a year per 1,000 connections, against **0.95** in the newest: about 51 times as many.
Relining has tripled since 2017 to about **800** connections a year, roughly 0.2% of the system; German cities renew about 1.1% of their sewers a year.
If nothing were renewed, connections past a typical life would grow from **32,720** today to **104,106** by 2076.

sections.heading: What this report asks, and how it answers
sections.text:
Calgary's sewers carry wastewater from every home and business to three treatment plants. Many were laid in the building boom of the 1950s to 1970s. This report asks two questions. How old is Calgary's sanitary sewer system? And how does that age compare with how long sewer pipes usually last around the world?

The City publishes its water mains as open data, with the year each was laid. It does not publish its sanitary sewer mains. It does publish every **public sanitary service connection**: the pipe from the street sewer to each property line, owned and maintained by the City. There are **368,085** of them, about **2,785 km** in all, each with the date it went in and its material.

A service connection is usually laid at the same time as the sewer main in the street it joins. So the age of the connections on a street is a fair guide to the age of the sewer under it. It is not a perfect one: a main can be relined or replaced without touching the connections, and the reverse. This report therefore speaks of the age of "the sewer system" as measured by its connections, and says so wherever it matters.

Ages are worked out to 2026. 396 connections have no date and 18 have a date after 2026; they are left out of the age figures, which use the other **367,671**.

The rest of the report runs in this order: the size of the system; when it was built; what it is made of; how long sewer pipes last elsewhere; how Calgary measures up; the wave of ageing still to come; where the oldest pipes are; whether older sewers back up more; and what renewal looks like today. Each chapter ends by saying what it means for the next.

sections.heading: The system at a glance
sections.text:
The City's Water Services reports that its wastewater system serves **over 1.4 million** Calgarians and regional customers. It runs **over 5,000 km** of underground pipes, **43** lift stations and **three** treatment plants: Bonnybrook, Fish Creek and Pine Creek. In 2023 the plants met Alberta's quality standards 100% of the time.

The public part of the service connections adds **2,785 km** of smaller pipe. **368,085** buildings are connected: mostly single-family homes, then duplexes, commercial buildings and triplexes.

Nearly all connections are 100 mm across (a 4-inch pipe). That uniformity matters: it means age and material, not size, are what set one connection apart from another. The next chapter looks at age.

sections.heading: When the system was built
sections.text:
Half of all connections went in before **1995** and half after. The typical connection is **31 years** old; the average is **34.4** years.

The building came in waves. The 1950s and 1960s added **54,152** connections. The 1970s were the busiest decade of all, with **60,506**. Growth slowed in the 1980s, then the 1990s and 2000s added **125,478** more as the suburbs spread.

Measured against today:

- **91,258** connections (24.8%) are more than 50 years old.
- **8,643** (2.4%) are more than 75 years old.
- **1,206** (0.3%) are more than 100 years old.
- **61,772** (16.8%) were built before 1970.

By world standards this is a young system, because Calgary grew so fast so late. But a young average hides an old core. The 1970s peak, the largest single group, turns 50 this decade. The next chapter shows that the pipes from each era are also made of different things, and the material decides how long they last.

sections.heading: What the pipes are made of
sections.text:
Calgary's connections fall into three generations of material.

- **Before 1955:** most records say "other" or give no material, with some cast iron. These 24,039 connections have a typical install year of **1953**. Many of these records also have no length, so they are among the least well described in the City's data.
- **1955 to the early 1980s: clay tile.** **74,089** connections (20.2%) are clay tile, nearly all laid from the 1950s to the 1970s (43,772 in the 1970s alone). Their typical install year is **1972**, so the typical clay connection is **54** years old. Cast iron (12,218 connections, typically 1965) and a material the City codes "TP" (7,595, typically 1957) belong to the same era. The dataset does not define "TP".
- **From the 1970s: PVC plastic.** PVC became common in the 1970s and is now **66.6%** of all connections, typically from **2003**.

A fourth group is the newest: **4,097** connections relined from inside with a cured-in-place liner (CIPP), most of them since 2017. Relining is how the City renews an old connection without digging it up; the dates on these records are the dates of relining.

Material matters because each lasts differently. The next chapter sets out how long each is expected to last, from utilities around the world.

sections.heading: How long sewer pipes usually last around the world
sections.text:
There is no single world figure for the life of a sewer pipe. Utilities set their own, from their records and engineering judgement, and the figures vary widely. What they agree on is the order: plastic and well-made clay and concrete last longest; cast iron, asbestos cement and unknown materials least.

- **Canada (a city's own plan).** The District of Saanich, BC, sets the life of a gravity sanitary main at 100 years for PVC, polyethylene, reinforced concrete and vitrified clay; 75 years for ductile iron and asbestos cement; and 45 years for unreinforced concrete, liners and unknown materials (2023).
- **Australia.** Sydney Water assumed 130 years for clay and concrete gravity sewers, 85 for PVC and iron, and 55 for asbestos cement. Its reviewers, Halcrow, gave typical ranges of 50 to 150 years for clay, 100 to 150 for plastics, 75 to 100 for concrete, 30 to 100 for iron and asbestos cement, and 50 to 75 for relining (2007).
- **United Kingdom.** Eight UK water companies used sewer lives from 40 to 200 years, most between 40 and 150.
- **Canada, all underground pipes.** Statistics Canada reports that new water, sewer and stormwater pipes laid in 2020 were expected to last 50 to 73 years.
- **Germany.** The national sewer survey found the average public sewer was 39.8 years old; in cities over 250,000 the average was 50 years, and more than 40% of the network was over 50. About 1.1% of the network was renewed each year (2015 survey).
- **Condition, not just age.** In Canada, 13% of sewer pipes under 450 mm were in poor or very poor condition in 2022. In the United States, wastewater earned a D+ in the 2025 national infrastructure report card.

Two lessons follow. Age alone does not prove a pipe has failed: Germany's survey notes century-old brick sewers still in good condition. But age and material together are the best guide a city has where it lacks inspections. This report therefore compares Calgary's connections against three lives for each material: a low one (the short end of the ranges), a typical one (the Canadian city figure) and a high one (the long end). The next chapter applies them.

sections.heading: Calgary's connections against those lives
sections.text:
Applying each material's life to each connection's age gives three answers, one for each view of how long pipes last.

- **Typical life:** **32,720** connections (8.9%) are already past it.
- **Low life:** **94,697** (25.8%) are past it.
- **High life:** **8,535** (2.3%) are past even that.

The difference between the views comes almost entirely from **clay tile**. At a typical life of 100 years, only 3 clay connections are past it. At the low life of 50 years, **55,915** are, three in four of all clay connections. So the question of how long Calgary's clay will last is the biggest single unknown in the system. Clay itself is durable; its weak points are the joints between short lengths, where roots and ground movement get in.

**Cast iron** is the clearest worry: **6,226** of its 12,218 connections are past a typical 60-year life. The "TP" and "other or not recorded" groups (31,634 connections) are past even a cautious 45 years almost entirely, because they are mostly from the 1940s and 1950s.

PVC is not a concern today: only 6 PVC connections are past 100 years, and those are early records that may be data errors.

These counts describe today. The next chapter looks ahead, because Calgary's busiest building decade is about to age into the same position.

sections.heading: The wave still to come
sections.text:
If nothing were renewed, the number of connections past their typical life would grow from **32,720** today to **43,747** by 2051 and **104,106** by 2076. On the cautious low lives, it would grow from **94,697** to **112,835** within five years, as the last of the 1970s clay passes 50, and to **169,885** by 2076.

The shape matters as much as the size. On typical lives, the count rises slowly until about 2056, then steeply, as the 1970s clay tile reaches 100 years and the 1990s and 2000s plastic reaches its own limits later. On low lives, most of the jump comes now, in the 2020s.

These projections are not forecasts of failure. They assume nothing is renewed, and that each material lasts exactly its benchmark life. Their use is to show the size of the job and when it lands. The next question is where in the city it lands.

sections.heading: Where the oldest sewers are
sections.text:
The map shades each community by the typical age of its sewer connections (the median: half are older, half newer). It covers the 211 communities with at least 50 connections; grey areas have fewer (mostly industrial land and the newest communities still being built). The communities are too many to label, so the tables below give the figures.

The pattern is a set of rings. The oldest sewers are in the inner city, built out from the centre before 1960. The middle ring of 1960s and 1970s suburbs is where the clay tile is. The outer suburbs, built since 1990, are on PVC and are young.

- The **Centre** sector is oldest: its communities' typical connection is 65 years old and 51.8% of its connections are over 50.
- The **Southeast** is youngest: typically about 20 years, with under 5% over 50.
- The 56 communities whose typical connection is **60 years or older** hold **53,807** connections.

The oldest are Rosedale (76 years), Scarboro, Cliff Bungalow, Upper Mount Royal, Ramsay and Inglewood, all with typical connections from the early 1950s. The table lists the twenty oldest with at least 200 connections, with the share past each community's typical life.

Age by itself is a measure of risk, not of failure. The next chapter asks whether older sewers actually cause more problems for residents.

sections.heading: Do older sewers back up more?
sections.text:
Residents report sewage back-ups to 311. Over the two years from October 2024 to September 2026 there were **12,835** back-up requests placed in a community: **17.45** a year for every 1,000 connections.

The rate climbs steeply with the age of the sewers:

- Communities whose typical connection is **0 to 14 years** old: **0.95** back-ups a year per 1,000 connections (26 communities).
- Communities whose typical connection is **15 to 29 years** old: **3.83** back-ups a year per 1,000 connections (39 communities).
- Communities whose typical connection is **30 to 44 years** old: **6.77** back-ups a year per 1,000 connections (28 communities).
- Communities whose typical connection is **45 to 59 years** old: **31.58** back-ups a year per 1,000 connections (46 communities).
- Communities whose typical connection is **60 years or more** old: **48.02** back-ups a year per 1,000 connections (56 communities).

That is about **51 times** the rate of the newest communities. Across the 195 communities with at least 200 connections, the rank correlation between typical age and the back-up rate is **0.883** (1 would be a perfect match), a very strong link.

Two cautions. First, a back-up request does not say where the blockage was: many are in the owner's part of the pipe, inside the property line, which is just as old as the City's part. Second, older communities differ in other ways too: mature trees whose roots get into joints, older basements, and older plumbing. So the link shows where problems are concentrated, not that the City's pipe is always the cause.

The highest rates are in Southview (136.86 a year per 1,000), Sunalta, Highwood, Forest Lawn and Greenview. Several, such as Greenview, Thorncliffe and Chinook Park, are clay-tile communities of the late 1950s and early 1960s, not the oldest in the city. That fits the clay-joint weakness described earlier, and points to where the low view of clay's life may be the right one.

Back-ups reported to 311 have held steady at about 6,600 to 7,500 a year since 2016. The ageing system has not yet shown up as a citywide rise; the strain is local. The next chapter looks at what the City is doing about it.

sections.heading: Renewal today, and what it can achieve
sections.text:
The City renews sewer connections in two ways: relining from inside (CIPP) and replacing. The open data shows both.

- **Relining** has picked up. Recorded relinings rose from about 250 a year in 2017 and 2018 to **833** in 2023, **682** in 2024 and **791** in 2025.
- **Replacement and rebuilding.** In the 82 communities whose typical connection dates from 1975 or earlier, **10,859** connections (10.3%) are new plastic or relined since 2010. Some of these are City renewals; many come with infill redevelopment, when a new home gets a new connection.

At around 800 relinings a year, the City relines about 0.2% of its connections each year. Germany's cities renew about 1.1% of their sewer network a year. Relining is not the only renewal, and the City's main-line work is not in the open data, so this is not a full comparison. But it does show the scale: at 800 a year, relining all 32,720 connections already past a typical life would take about 41 years.

Calgary's water mains show what sustained renewal can do. Water main breaks fell from **535** in 2001 to **160** in 2025, a fall of 70%, after years of replacing and relining cast iron. The water network is similar in age to the sewer connections: its typical main dates from 1990, 26.5% of its 5,391 km is over 50, and 774 km is still cast iron.

The City's own risk reports add the large pipes this data cannot see. Nine large wastewater river crossings are of unknown condition, rated a severe risk, with about **$400 million** needed over ten years. In 2023 the wastewater collection and treatment capital budget was **$263.9 million**, of which 44.5% was spent in the year.

conclusion:
Calgary's sewer system is young on average and old at its core. Measured by its 368,085 public service connections, the typical sewer is 31 years old, younger than Germany's city networks, because Calgary built so much so recently. The chapter on when the system was built showed the waves behind that average: an inner city laid before 1960, a 1950s-to-1970s boom, and young suburbs since 1990.

The chapter on materials showed that each wave used a different pipe: unrecorded materials and cast iron first, clay tile in the boom, PVC since. The world benchmarks showed that utilities expect plastic and clay to last about a century, and cast iron, unknown and relined pipe far less. Put together, 32,720 connections are past a typical life today, mostly the old cast iron and unrecorded pipe of the inner city. On cautious lives the count is 94,697, and the difference is the 1970s clay tile. The wave chapter showed that this decade is when the cautious view bites, and the 2050s and 2060s when the typical view does.

The map placed that risk in rings: oldest in the Centre, clay in the middle suburbs, young in the outer ones. The back-up chapter then showed the risk is not only on paper: back-ups run about 51 times as often in the oldest communities as in the newest, and some of the worst rates are in 1960s clay-tile communities, which supports the cautious view of clay. The renewal chapter showed the City has stepped up relining, and the water mains show that sustained renewal works, cutting breaks by 70%. But at today's pace, relining alone would take decades to reach the connections already past a typical life.

The thread through every chapter is the same: Calgary's sewer problem is not yet citywide, but it is concentrated, predictable from age and material, and about to grow as the largest building decade ages. The data to plan for it exists for connections; the missing piece is the same open record for the sewer mains themselves.
method: Every public sanitary service connection in the City's open data (xesp-3jc3, 368,085 records, read November 7, 2026) was placed in its community by the start point of its line, using the City's community boundaries (surr-xmvs).
Ages are 2026 minus the install year. 396 records with no date and 18 dated after 2026 are left out of age figures (367,671 used).

Materials were grouped: PVC; other plastic (PLA, HDPE, PEX, PE); clay tile (TIL); cast iron (CI, DI); concrete (CON); relined (CIPP); TP (as coded, not defined in the dataset); other or not recorded (OTHER and blank).
Each connection was compared with a low, typical and high expected life for its material (table in chapter 5). 'Past its life' means its age is greater than that life.
The wave projection repeats the comparison for future years, assuming no renewal.
Typical age of a community is the median age of its connections. The map shows communities with at least 50 connections; rankings and the back-up analysis use those with at least 200.

Sewage back-ups are 311 requests of type 'WATS - Sewage Back-up' (open data iahh-g8bj), without duplicates, October 1, 2024 to September 30, 2026, by community; rates are per 1,000 connections a year. The rank correlation is Spearman's, across communities.
Water mains (w6h9-w33i, active mains) and water main breaks (dpcu-jr23) are used for comparison.

limitations: The City does not publish its sanitary sewer mains as open data. Service connections are used as a guide to the age of the sewer in each street; a main may have been relined or replaced separately.
Material is not recorded for 24,039 connections, and the code 'TP' (7,595) is not defined in the dataset. Many of these records also lack a length.
Expected lives are benchmarks from other utilities, not inspections. Actual life depends on soil, installation, joints, roots and flows. Age is a guide to risk, not proof of failure.
Sewage back-up requests include blockages in the owner's part of the pipe; they show where problems are concentrated, not who owns the cause.
Renewal of sewer mains, and replacements not recorded as a new connection, are not in the open data, so the renewal rate here is a partial view.
Large trunk sewers, river crossings, lift stations and plants are outside this data; the City's own risk report is quoted for them.

recommendations.title: Publish the sanitary sewer main inventory as open data
recommendations.detail: The water main inventory is already open (install year, material, length). The same record for sanitary mains would let anyone check the age and material of the pipe under each street, not just the connections.
recommendations.evidence: Chapter 1 and the limitations: only connections are published.

recommendations.title: Settle the life of 1960s and 1970s clay tile with targeted inspection
recommendations.detail: Clay tile is 74,089 connections and decides whether 61,977 more connections are past their life. Camera inspection of a sample in the clay communities with the highest back-up rates (Greenview, Thorncliffe, Chinook Park) would show which view of clay's life applies in Calgary.
recommendations.evidence: Chapters 6 and 9: the low/typical gap is clay; some of the highest back-up rates are clay communities.

recommendations.title: Define and fill in the unknown materials
recommendations.detail: 31,634 connections, mostly from the 1940s and 1950s, have no material or the undefined code 'TP'. They are the oldest group and the least described.

recommendations.title: Weigh relining priority by back-up rate as well as age
recommendations.detail: The 56 communities with a typical connection of 60 years or more report 48.02 back-ups a year per 1,000 connections. Ranking relining by back-ups per connection, not age alone, would put Southview, Sunalta, Highwood and Forest Lawn ahead of some older but quieter communities.

action_plan.action: Ask Water Services whether the sanitary main inventory can be published like the water main inventory
action_plan.measure: A sanitary main dataset on the open data portal

action_plan.action: Request the results of any CCTV inspection of clay-tile connections and mains, by community
action_plan.measure: A Calgary-specific life for clay tile in the next asset plan

action_plan.action: Track back-ups per 1,000 connections by community each year
action_plan.measure: Rates falling in the communities with the highest rates today
